en: *Mahāyāna-śatadharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra: A Brief Record of Names and Numbers from the Mūla-prakaraṇa*,
composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. As the World-Honored One has said, "All dharmas are without self.
What are all dharmas? In what sense are they without self?
All phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are, in brief, of five kinds:

first, mental phenomena (*cittadharma*); second, mental concomitants (*caitasikadharma*); third, material phenomena (*rūpadharma*); fourth, formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāradharma*); and fifth, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).

Because it is the most excellent of all; because it is associated with this [nature]; because it is the reflected image manifested by both; because it is the differentiation of the three stages; and because it is that which is revealed.
In this sequential order, the first category,
the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), consists briefly of eight types:

(1) eye-consciousness, (2) ear-consciousness, (3) nose-consciousness, (4) tongue-consciousness, (5) body-consciousness, (6) mind-consciousness, (7) *manas*-consciousness, and (8) *ālaya*-consciousness.
The second category, the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), comprises fifty-one types in brief, which are divided into six groups:

first, five omnipresent factors; second, five object-specific factors; third, eleven wholesome factors; fourth, six afflictions; fifth, twenty secondary afflictions; and sixth, four indeterminate factors.
The five universal mental factors are: first, attention; second, contact; third, sensation; fourth, perception; and fifth, volition.
The five object-specific mental factors are: first, desire; second, resolve; third, mindfulness; fourth, concentration; and fifth, wisdom.

The eleven wholesome factors are: first, faith; second, diligence; third, shame; fourth, remorse; fifth, non-attachment; sixth, non-hatred; seventh, non-delusion; eighth, pliancy; ninth, heedfulness; tenth, equanimity; and eleventh, non-harming.
The six root afflictions (*kleśa*) are: first, greed; second, anger; third, pride; fourth, ignorance; fifth, doubt; and sixth, wrong view.

The twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are: first, rage; second, resentment; third, vexation; fourth, concealment; fifth, deception; sixth, guile; seventh, arrogance; eighth, harmfulness; ninth, envy; tenth, stinginess; eleventh, lack of shame; twelfth, lack of dread of blame; thirteenth, lack of faith; fourteenth, laziness; fifteenth, heedlessness; sixteenth, lethargy; seventeenth, restlessness; eighteenth, loss of mindfulness; nineteenth, lack of clear comprehension; and twentieth, distraction.
The four indeterminate factors are: first, torpor; second, regret; third, vitarka; and fourth, vicāra.
Third, the material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are briefly of eleven kinds:

first, the eye; second, the ear; third, the nose; fourth, the tongue; fifth, the body; sixth, visible form; seventh, sound; eighth, odor; ninth, taste; tenth, tangibility; and eleventh, matter subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The fourth category, the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*), comprises briefly twenty-four types: (1) acquisition (*prāpti*); (2) life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*);

(3) generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*); (4) the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*); (5) the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); (6) the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); (7) the retribution of non-conception (*āsaṃjñika*); (8) the collection of names (*nāma-kāya*); (9) the collection of phrases (*pada-kāya*); (10) the collection of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*); (11) birth (*jāti*); (12) aging (*jarā*); (13) duration (*sthiti*); (14) impermanence (*anityatā*); (15) transmigration (*pravṛtti*); (16) specific determination (*pratiniyama*); (17) association (*yoga*); (18) rapidity (*java*); (19) succession (*anukrama*); (20) spatial direction (*deśa*); (21) time (*kāla*); (22) number (*saṃkhyā*); (23) the nature of combination (*sāmagrī*); and (24) the nature of non-combination (*asāmagrī*).
The fifth category, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), briefly comprises six types:

first, the unconditioned of space (*ākāśa-asaṃskṛta*); second, the unconditioned of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*); third, the unconditioned of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the unconditioned of imperturbable cessation (*āniñjya-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*); fifth, the unconditioned of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*); and sixth, the unconditioned of suchness (*tathatā-asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding the statement "there is no self," there are briefly two types:
first, the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*); second, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
*The Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna*.
